newsitem.title: CHINA: Year-end money squeeze to depress new China bond.
newsitem.headline: Year-end money squeeze to depress new China bond.

text.p: Demand for tighter liquidity as year-end approaches and a bull run on China's stock markets will depress the price of its first seven-year treasury bond, to be listed on Thursday, analysts said.

The bond, the last batch of China's state debt issue this year, was likely to be the first bond issued this year to trade below its issue price, of 100 yuan ($12), despite offering a higher return than bank deposits, analysts said on Wednesday.
The coupon on the bond was set at 8.56 percent, 1.09 percentage points higher than the annual rate of 7.47 percent for one-year bank deposits.
"The central bank has instructed state banks and financial institutions to do a good job of controlling money supply with the approach of the year-end," said a T-bill trader.
"This is a routine procedure by the central government to reduce the annual money supply," he said.

China's broad M2 supply had increased by a year-on-year 26.9 percent at the end of September, against a target of 25 percent and against full 1995 M2 growth of 29.5 percent. Firms have in recent years increased spending in the last quarter.

A total of 20 billion yuan worth of seven-year T-bonds was issued from November 1 to Wednesday. The bonds will be listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges on Thursday. It is the first time China has issued a seven-year bond.
Interest on the new bond will be calculated as from November 1 and paid on an annual basis instead of at maturity, allowing buyers to re-invest their money during the life of the bond.
In the first few days of issue, this high return and promise of liquidity made the bond attractive to individual investors.

But it has become increasingly less attractive as the listing date draws near. Underwriters wanted to sell to raise money to meet monetary requirements set by the central bank before the end of the year, industry sources said.
The underwriters were bearish about the short-term prospects for the bond market and expected the new bond to fall, they said.

In the past few weeks, Shanghai's T-bond spot market, China's largest, has been falling mainly because of the liquidity squeeze and expectations that coupons for new treasury bonds will go down due to falling bank interest rates.
The central bank cut interest rates in May and August with the annual rate for one-year fixed deposits reduced to 7.47 percent from a high 10.98 percent up to May.
Another bearish factor for the T-bond was a bull-run on China's two domestic A share markets since April, which had sucked money from the T-bond spot market, traders said.
In Shanghai, the most active 10-year bond, a market barometer, had fallen to 120 yuan this week from 127 yuan in early November, indicating the weak sentiment, they said.
"The seven-year bond is being listed at a difficult time and its price is likely to stay at low levels for a few months," one trader said.
